name: Funder Formatting and Compliance
title: Funder Formatting and Compliance
answer: Funder formatting and compliance covers the rules a funding body sets for how a proposal must look, what it must contain, and how it must be submitted. It includes page limits, font and margin requirements, required sections, budget tables, biographical sketches, reference styles, file naming, and deadlines. It also covers eligibility checks, required certifications, and the difference between a funder's general instructions and a specific call's instructions. In practice, this work sits between the research idea and the submission portal, and it determines whether a proposal is reviewed or returned without review.

sections.body: Funder formatting and compliance covers the rules a funding body sets for how a proposal must look, what it must contain, and how it must be submitted. It includes page limits, font and margin requirements, required sections, budget tables, biographical sketches, reference styles, file naming, and deadlines. It also covers eligibility checks, required certifications, and the difference between a funder's general instructions and a specific call's instructions. In practice, this work sits between the research idea and the submission portal, and it determines whether a proposal is reviewed or returned without review.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on funder portals and grants management systems, such as Grants.gov, NIH eRA Commons, NSF Research.gov, and the EU Funding and Tenders Portal. Institutions often add their own systems for routing, internal deadlines, budget approval, and document storage. Common tools include word processors, reference managers, PDF generators, spreadsheet budgets, and version control or shared drives. Validation software checks file type, page count, font embedding, and required fields before the portal accepts a submission.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical workflow starts with a close reading of the funding call and the creation of a compliance matrix that maps every requirement to a section, an owner, and a deadline. Writers draft in templates, then reviewers check page limits, headings, citations, budget justification, and required attachments against the funder's instructions. Research offices run internal reviews, collect signatures, and confirm that the budget matches the project narrative and the sponsor's allowable costs. Before submission, teams validate the PDF, check file names, and submit early enough to resolve portal errors. After submission, they archive the submitted version, confirmations, and correspondence for later reporting or audit.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on accuracy, authorization, and provenance. Institutions certify that the proposal is true, that the people named have agreed to participate, and that required approvals for human subjects, animals, data management, ethics, or export control are in place. Funders and institutions keep audit trails of versions, approvals, and communications, because a false certification or a missing disclosure can lead to rejection, funding delays, or sanctions. Provenance matters for every claim, citation, and preliminary result, so teams retain source documents, data, and permissions. Open access terms, intellectual property clauses, and data sharing policies also shape what can be promised in the proposal and what must be delivered later.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward structured, machine readable proposals and automated compliance checks. Funders are experimenting with application programming interfaces, persistent identifiers such as ORCID and DOI, and systems that validate budgets and biosketches at the point of entry. AI assisted drafting and review are entering the workflow, which raises questions about disclosure, authorship, and hallucinated citations. Policies on the use of generative AI in proposals are still uneven across funders, and many institutions now require a human check of every generated sentence and reference. The likely result is faster administrative screening, but also more explicit rules about what must be declared and what must be traceable.
